{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=relationship+between+constructive+expansion+self-correction+and+safety+failure+modes+in+multi-turn+reasoning+models&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1\", \"title\": [\"Reflective Reasoning System: Inference-Time Self-Diagnosis and Self-Correction for Large Reasoning Models\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often exhibit an efficiency-accuracy trade-off, leading to errors from insufficient self-diagnosis and correction during inference. Existing reasoning methods frequently lack internal feedback for refining generated steps. To address this, we propose the Reflective Reasoning System (RRS), an inference-time framework integrating explicit self-diagnosis and self-correction loops into LRM reasoning. RRS strategically employs meta-cognitive tokens to guide the model through initial reasoning, critical self-assessment of potential flaws, and subsequent revision, all without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. Our extensive experiments across diverse open-source models and challenging benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and scientific reasoning demonstrate that RRS consistently achieves significant accuracy improvements compared to baseline models and competitive inference-time enhancement methods. Human evaluations and ablation studies further confirm the efficacy of these distinct self-diagnosis and self-correction phases, highlighting RRS's ability to unlock LRMs' latent reflective capabilities for more robust and accurate solutions.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 12, 19]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"title\": [\"Structural Simulation Benchmark for Reasoning Large Language Models: Accuracy, Reliability, and Failure Modes\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs), particularly reasoning-oriented models optimized for long-horizon and multi-step inference, are increasingly used to assist programming and scientific research. However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1201/b15938-120\", \"title\": [\"Modeling the relationship between wind turbine failure modes and the environment\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1201/b15938-120\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 9, 18]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6482082\", \"title\": [\"Multi-Turn Constraint Persistence (MTCP): Benchmarking Post-Correction Reliability in Large Language Models\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Most evaluations of large language model (LLM) instruction-following test single-turn compliance: a model receives a prompt and its response is scored. This design does not capture post-correction reliability, the capacity to maintain a constraint after it has been explicitly corrected within the same conversation. This paper introduces the Multi-Turn Constraint Persistence (MTCP) benchmark, a structured protocol isolating and measuring this property. MTCP uses deterministic three-turn probe sequences and automated violation detection across five evaluation vectors: Negative Constraint Adherence (NCA), Structural Format Compliance (SFC), Information Density and Length (IDL), Contextual Grounding (CG), and Multilingual Consistency (LANG). The benchmark was applied to twenty-seven production models from twelve providers: xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Google, AWS Bedrock, Cohere, Mistral, Cerebras, DeepSeek, and OpenRouter. 29,352 probe evaluations were conducted across 142 benchmark runs. Pass rates range from 90.5% (grok-3-mini, Grade A) to 47.0% (mistral-small-3.2, Grade F). Newer frontier models do not outperform predecessors: GPT-4o scores 22.8 percentage points below GPT-4o-mini. No model achieves a passing grade. Control probe evaluation across 20 previously undisclosed probes shows substantial performance degradation in all models, with scores collapsing to a 10-57.5% band. DeepSeek-R1 is the exception, with a 5 percentage point drop. The benchmark produces structured, auditable evaluation records relevant to EU Artificial Intelligence Act compliance documentation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6482082\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "b1ffe82019b87b59e47b3f933cc66c06054698e9957360cd748a6f277e0ca693", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "doi:10.1201/b15938-120", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6482082"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "https://doi.org/10.1201/b15938-120", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6482082"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
